label: Adiabatic Invariants
notes: Open by separating two clocks: the fast oscillation period and the slow drift of a parameter. The whole appendix lives in the gap between them. Promise the punchline now: one geometric quantity, the area swept in phase space, survives the slow change almost untouched, and that survivor is the action.

label: Two Time Scales
notes: Make the small parameter explicit. Let the parameter change on a time of order one over epsilon while the system oscillates on a time of order one. Stress that adiabatic means slow relative to the oscillation, not slow in absolute terms. Everything that follows is an expansion in this ratio epsilon.

label: Action of an Oscillator
notes: Define the action as the phase-space area enclosed by one closed orbit divided by two pi. Emphasize it is a function of the orbit, hence of energy and the frozen parameter. Contrast it with energy, which is not conserved when the parameter moves; the action is the quantity engineered to be robust.

label: Frozen Orbits
notes: Introduce the freezing trick: hold the parameter fixed and the motion is exactly periodic with a well-defined closed orbit. The action is computed on that frozen orbit. As the parameter slowly creeps, imagine a slowly relabeled family of frozen orbits, and ask which orbit the true trajectory sits on at each instant.

label: The Invariance Theorem
notes: State the central result carefully. Over a slow smooth change of the parameter, the action returns nearly to its starting value; the change is bounded by the rate epsilon and, for smooth changes over a full passage, is exponentially small. Energy and amplitude may swing wildly, but the action barely notices.

label: Area Is Preserved
notes: Drive the picture home. As the potential well deforms, the orbit changes shape, but the area it encloses is conserved. This is the geometric heart of the theorem: Liouville-type area preservation under slow deformation. Have students trace one loop deforming into another while the enclosed area stays the same.

label: Pendulum on a Shortening String
notes: Walk through the canonical example. Pull the string of a swinging pendulum slowly through the pivot. The frequency rises, the energy rises, the amplitude in angle grows, yet the ratio of energy to frequency stays fixed. That fixed ratio is exactly the action, and the example makes the abstract invariant tangible.

label: Energy Tracks Frequency
notes: Quantify the pendulum. For a slow harmonic-like oscillator the action equals energy over frequency, so energy is proportional to frequency. Halve the string length, the frequency goes up by root two, and the energy follows. Stress that no energy is conserved here; the conserved object is the dimensionless action.

label: Charged Particle in a Field
notes: Move to the magnetic example. A charged particle gyrates around field lines; the magnetic moment, the action of that gyration, is adiabatically invariant as the field strength slowly varies along the path. Connect the magnetic moment to the same action integral so students see one theorem behind two physical settings.

label: Magnetic Mirrors
notes: Show the application. As the particle drifts into a stronger field, conservation of the magnetic moment forces perpendicular energy up and parallel energy down until the parallel motion reverses. That reflection is the magnetic mirror, the principle behind mirror confinement and the trapping of particles in planetary radiation belts.

label: Synthesis
notes: Close by tying the thread. Two time scales create the regime; the action, an area in phase space, is the invariant; area preservation under slow deformation is the mechanism; pendulum and gyrating particle are the witnesses. Leave students with the slogan: when parameters change slowly, geometry remembers the area.
